title: Even his back ached
hook: the old Buddha warms his back in the sun; Ananda sees his skin loosen
tomorrow: A friend gives the hard thing

segments.voice: Yesterday: six ways to be dear, kindness in public and in private, and the shared bowl. Did you do one unseen kindness? Today, one of the tenderest scenes in the canon. Day six hundred seventy-six.

Late afternoon in Savatthi, at the Eastern Park, in the mansion of Migara's mother, the great hall the laywoman Visakha gave to the community. The Buddha has come out of his afternoon seclusion. He's an old man now. He sits in the western sun, warming his back. Ananda, his attendant for many years, comes over and begins to rub his limbs with his hands. Anyone who has cared for an aging parent knows this moment: your hands on their arms, and suddenly you notice how thin the skin has become. Ananda notices. And he says it out loud. Today: even his back ached.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE SUN.` → `ANANDA RUBS HIS LIMBS.` → `HE NOTICES.`

segments.voice: It's wonderful, sir, Ananda says, it's amazing. Your complexion is no longer clear and bright. Your limbs are slack and wrinkled. Your body is bent forward. And there's a change in your senses: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body. Imagine saying that to your teacher. But the Buddha doesn't flinch. So it is, Ananda, he says. In youth one is subject to aging; in health, to sickness; in life, to death. The complexion is no longer clear, the limbs are slack, the body is bent, the senses change. Then he speaks a verse that turns on aging itself, scolding it: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. Even someone who lives a hundred years, he says, is bound for death; aging spares no one, it crushes everything. And then, the text says, he gets up, and goes into town for alms. That last detail is the whole teaching. He names it, he grieves it a little in verse, and then he goes on with the day. Elsewhere in the canon there are other glimpses: a day when his back hurts and he asks Sariputta to teach in his place while he lies down to rest it. The texts don't hide the Buddha's body. They show it aging, aching, ordinary. Many Buddhists find that a comfort. Awakening, in this telling, didn't exempt even him from an old man's back. Even his.
screen: `YOUR SKIN IS LOOSE, SIR.` · `SO IT IS, ANANDA.` · `A VERSE AGAINST OLD AGE.` · then, large: `THEN HE GOES FOR ALMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for an aging body. It might be your own, or someone else's. Sit, and turn your back toward a window or a warm lamp if you can. Let your hands rest on your forearms, and feel the skin, the warmth, the years in it. Breathe. Then bring to mind someone older whom you love. Picture warming their back, rubbing their arms, without hurry. Notice what tenderness feels like. Then think of one real thing you could do for an aging body this week, yours or theirs. The bell holds the time.
Even his back ached. The old Buddha in the evening sun, Ananda noticing his body's age, and the answer: so it is. Today's word.
Your line: even his. Today, when your body creaks or someone you love slows down, remember: even his, and then go on with the day, gently. Day six hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell this scene when teaching on aging and impermanence, and caring for elders, including elderly monks and nuns, is held up across Buddhist cultures as a meritorious act.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. rubbing your teacher's arms, you see how old his body has become. what do you do?
options: say nothing; it would be disrespectful.
say it out loud: how changed you are.
fork.reveal: Ananda says it plainly, and the Buddha agrees: so it is. aging spares no one. then he gets up and goes for alms.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit jara: old age, aging; the first of the three messengers in the Buddha's story.

trapdoor: what you thought: an awakened being would be beyond aches and pains.
what it means: in SN 48.41 the Buddha's body ages like anyone's, and he says so.
what a scholar hears: the scene sits in the Connected Sayings on the faculties, because aging shows itself in the failing of the five senses.
